answer_text:
Let \(F_2=\langle a,b\rangle=\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z\).

**Upper bound.**  
\(F_2\) is countable, since its elements are finite words in the finite alphabet
\(\{a,a^{-1},b,b^{-1}\}\). Therefore the set of all subgroups of \(F_2\) is a subset of the power set \(\mathcal P(F_2)\), so

\[
|\operatorname{Sub}(F_2)|\le |\mathcal P(F_2)|=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

**Lower bound.**  
Define a homomorphism

\[
\varphi:F_2\to \mathbb Z
\]

by \(\varphi(a)=0\), \(\varphi(b)=1\). Let \(K=\ker\varphi\). By the Nielsen–Schreier theorem, \(K\) is a free group. More explicitly, using the Schreier transversal \(\{b^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}\), a free basis for \(K\) is

\[
\{x_n=b^nab^{-n}:n\in\mathbb Z\}.
\]

Thus \(K\) is a free subgroup of \(F_2\) of countably infinite rank.

For every subset \(S\subseteq \mathbb Z\), define

\[
H_S=\langle x_n:n\in S\rangle \le K\le F_2.
\]

There are \(2^{\aleph_0}\) subsets \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z\). We claim the corresponding subgroups \(H_S\) are all distinct.

If \(S\ne T\), choose \(n\in T\setminus S\). Then \(x_n\in H_T\). But \(x_n\notin H_S\): since \(\{x_m:m\in\mathbb Z\}\) is a free basis of \(K\), there is a homomorphism \(K\to\mathbb Z\) sending \(x_n\mapsto 1\) and all other \(x_m\mapsto 0\). This homomorphism sends every generator of \(H_S\) to \(0\), hence sends \(H_S\) into \(0\), but sends \(x_n\) to \(1\). Therefore \(x_n\notin H_S\), so \(H_S\ne H_T\).

Hence there are at least \(2^{\aleph_0}\) subgroups of \(F_2\).

Combining the upper and lower bounds,

\[
|\operatorname{Sub}(F_2)|=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

\[
\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}
\]
